RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Lecture Introduction Finishing and Polishing
Finishing Makes the Shape. Polishing Makes the Shine.
Every restoration leaves the bur or the mill rough, over-contoured, and scratched. Two different processes fix that, and they are not interchangeable. Tap each one, then try the quick check.
Goal
Form
Contours, margins, embrasures, occlusion. Remove excess and the defects left by contouring.
Abrasive size
8 to 60 μm
Fluted carbides, fine diamonds, medium and fine discs, white stones.
Scratch pattern
One way per grit
Turned 90° at each grit, so leftover scratches show.
Force
Moderate
Enough to remove material, still with coolant and intermittent contact.
Sculptor. Finishing removes material on purpose: it establishes the anatomy and a blemish-free, well-adapted margin. It leaves scratches in one planned direction; that is expected.
Quick check A resin composite feels smooth to the explorer but looks dull. Which step was skipped?

Abrasives and instruments

01
Movement One
Why Bother?
A rough restoration is uncomfortable, collects plaque, wears the opposing tooth, and is weaker than it should be.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Benefits Surface Roughness in Numbers
Patients Feel a Roughness Difference of Half a Micron
Comfort, gingival health, chewing efficiency, and esthetics. Each has a roughness number behind it.
0.2 μm
Plaque retention threshold
Below this Ra, further smoothing no longer reduces bacterial retention. The polishing target.
0.25 to 0.5 μm
Tongue detection
Patients feel differences this small. The old estimate was 20 μm.
> 1 μm
Adhesion and staining
Bacteria adhere, stain collects, and metals tarnish and corrode.
Source: Phillips Ch. 16; Bollen et al. 1997; Jones et al. 2004. Ra is the mean profile roughness.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Wear and Strength Tribology and Fracture
Rough Ceramic Wears Enamel, and Its Surface Flaws Concentrate Stress
Rough
Wears the antagonist, weakens the restoration
Rough ceramic abrades opposing enamel and restorations; contacts and vertical dimension are lost.
Surface flaws concentrate stress. Chipping starts there, especially in unsupported veneering ceramic.
Polished
Kinder to enamel, more fatigue resistant
Polished zirconia and lithium disilicate wear enamel no more than enamel does (Lawson et al. 2014).
Removing surface flaws improves the cyclic fatigue strength of CAD-CAM ceramics (Nakazato et al. 1999).
Source: Phillips Ch. 16; Lawson et al. 2014; Nakazato et al. 1999.
02
Movement Two
Vocabulary and Mechanics
Four words on one continuum of abrasive wear. The two you will confuse most are finishing and polishing.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Four Procedures Cut, Grind, Finish, Polish
Each Step Uses Finer Grains and Lighter Force, and Only Polishing Erases the Pattern
All four are abrasive wear. Direct restorations usually skip cutting.
1 · Bulk reduction
Cutting
A bladed instrument shears material: carbide or steel bur, separating disc.
RemovesMost
PatternGrooves, one way
2 · Contouring
Grinding
Many random abrasive points: diamond burs, stones, coarse discs.
Abrasive~30 to 100 μm
PatternScratches, one way
3 · Defect removal
Finishing
Removes contouring scratches and marginal defects; defines anatomy and the margin.
Abrasive~8 to 60 μm
StrokeOne way per grit
4 · Luster
Polishing
Grains of 5 μm or less on an elastic backing; lightest force; almost nothing removed.
Abrasive≤ 5 μm
PatternEvery direction
When is polishing done?
When the finest abrasive no longer changes the luster. No scratches are visible; under magnification some always remain.
Source: Phillips Ch. 16 (key terms; Cutting, Grinding, Finishing, Polishing) and Table 16-1.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Finishing Versus Polishing The Distinction This Lecture Is Built On
Finishing Is Subtractive Shaping; Polishing Is Optical Refinement
Finishing
"Is the shape right?"
Purpose: contours, embrasures, occlusion, a smooth and well-adapted margin.
Tools: fine burs and stones, medium and fine discs and strips, coarse rubber points.
Stroke: one direction per grit, turned 90° at the next, so leftover scratches show.
Failure: ledges, open margins, flat spots, ditched cementum.
Polishing
"Does it shine?"
Purpose: luster and a surface under 0.2 μm; the form does not change.
Tools: superfine discs, fine rubber polishers, brushes, felt and pastes.
Stroke: every direction; the final scratches are too small to see.
Failure: dull surface, early stain, plaque, a patient who feels it.
The trap: polishing cannot fix a finishing problem. Paste over a ledge makes a shiny ledge.
Source: Phillips Ch. 16 (key terms; Finishing and Polishing Procedures).
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Modes of Abrasive Wear Tribology: Where the Grain Lives
Two-Body, Three-Body, and Erosion Differ in How the Grain Is Held
Hard particles plow grooves in a softer surface; the debris is the wear.
Two-body
Grain fixed to the tool
Burs, coated discs, rubber points. Efficient and directional.
Three-body
Loose grains between surfaces
Paste in a cup, pumice on a rag wheel. Grains tumble and plow in every direction: this is how luster is made.
Erosion
Grains carried by air or water
Air-particle abrasion. Chemical erosion (acid etching) is a bonding step, not a finishing method.
The modes cross over: a grain lost from a bur becomes three-body; a paste grain trapped in a cup acts two-body. Air abrasion in practice: 25 to 30 μm alumina for preparation, 50 μm to roughen intaglio surfaces before bonding, glass beads or sand to clean castings.
Source: Phillips Ch. 16, Mechanics of Abrasive Procedures, Fig. 16-2.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Lubrication Tribology: Friction and Heat
Too Little Lubricant Heats the Surface; Too Much Stops the Cut
What the lubricant does
water, glycerin, silicone oil; water-soluble intraorally
CoolsRemoves frictional heat
FlushesClears debris from the interface
StabilizesKeeps two-body from drifting to three-body
Too littleHeat rises, cutting drops
Too muchGrain loses contact, cutting drops
Handling rules
pastes and handpieces
Alumina pasteAdd water as the grit gets finer
Diamond pasteRun relatively dry
Bur directionMove against the rotation for a controlled cut
Proximal, subgingivalReciprocating handpiece
Source: Phillips Ch. 16, Abrasion, Abrasive Motion, Nonbonded Abrasives.

Grit and Grain Behavior Particle Size and Grain Fracture
A Good Abrasive Fractures to Stay Sharp; Diamond Is the Exception
Green coarse · ~150 μmBlue medium · ~100 μmRed fine · ~40 μmYellow superfine · ~15 μmWhite ultrafine · ~8 μm
Grain behavior
Fracture, do not dull: irregular grains break to expose fresh edges; SiC and garnet do this well.
Diamond is different: it wears at the tip and clogs on soft materials; best on enamel and ceramics.
Coarser is not faster: deep scratches later grits cannot remove, and subsurface damage in zirconia and lithium silicates.

Common Abrasives Hardness Matched to Substrate
Synthetic Abrasives Win on Predictability; Each Has a Home Substrate
Al₂O₃ · KHN 2100
Aluminum oxide
White stones, coated discs, air-abrasion powder, pastes. Harder than both resin composite matrix and filler, so it anchors most composite systems.
SiC · KHN 2500
Silicon carbide
Self-sharpening grains in green stones and rubber points. Alloys, ceramics, acrylic.
KHN 7000 to 10000
Diamond
Hardest known; synthetic is uniform and cheaper. Burs, strips, and pastes for tooth, ceramics, resin composite.
KHN 460 to 560
Pumice
Volcanic glass as slurry or in rubber points. Denture bases, enamel, amalgam, acrylic.
SnO₂
Tin oxide
Very fine paste. Final polish of enamel and metal in the mouth.
Fe₂O₃, silica
Rouge and tripoli
Fine abrasives in binder bars on rag wheels. Tripoli for alloys and acrylic; rouge for gold.
ZrSiO₄
Zirconium silicate
Discs, strips, and most prophy pastes.
CaCO₃
Chalk and cuttle
Mild. Chalk for enamel, amalgam, acrylic; cuttle discs for metal margins.
Source: Phillips Ch. 16, Types of Abrasives and Table 16-2.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Instrument Design Binder Strength and Grain Retention
The Binder Has One Job: Hold the Grain Just Long Enough, Then Let It Go
Class 1
Bonded
Grains in a binder, molded into points, wheels, cups. Vitreous (rigid, heat resistant), resinoid, rubber (latex: remove residue), metal (holds diamond, acts as a heat sink).
Class 2
Coated
Grains glued to paper, Mylar, or metal: discs and strips. Moisture-resistant backings stay stiff when wet. Metal strips for tight contacts; plastic strips for resin-based materials.
Class 3
Nonbonded
Loose grains in a paste or slurry on a nonabrasive carrier (cup, felt, brush), or propelled by air. Prophy and polishing pastes, pumice, air-abrasion powder.
Binder strength must match the substrate
Released too early, the tool wastes away; held too long, it clogs and heats. Alloys and ceramics need stronger binders: a composite disc on metal only polishes, because its binder is weak.

RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Bonded Tools in Service Truing, Dressing, Blinding
A Wobbling, Clogged Stone Cuts Less and Heats More
Before use
Truing
Run against a harder block until the stone spins without wobble. An out-of-round stone chatters and gouges.
Before and during
Dressing
Reshapes the tool and strips clogged debris to restore cutting.
The problem
Abrasive blinding
Debris fills the gaps between grains: cutting drops, heat rises. The stone looks coated with the substrate.
Diamond instruments come trued. Clean them for 2 to 4 s on a wet cleaning stone, but never finishing diamonds, which lose their grains.
Source: Phillips Ch. 16, Bonded Abrasives, Figs. 16-11 and 16-12.

Movement Four
Universal Rules
Whatever the material, the same protocol applies. Skip a grit and the coarse scratches never leave.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
The Universal Protocol Sequence and Direction
Each Grit Must Erase the Previous Grit's Scratches, So No Step Can Be Skipped
Tap the steps in order and watch the scratches shrink and turn 90°. Then try skipping a grit.
ContouredRa ≈ 3.0 μm
Start. The contoured surface carries deep scratches in one direction. Each next grit must be fine enough to shrink them and coarse enough to remove them.
Source: Phillips Ch. 16, Resin-Based Composite Restorations and Summary and Recommendations.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Habits What the Sequence Alone Does Not Guarantee
A Stray Coarse Grain Scratches Through the Final Step, So Keep Everything Clean
Five habits
Phillips, Summary and Recommendations
PressureLighter at the end of each grit; same grit, finer surface
RinseBetween grits, to remove debris and stray coarse grains
CarriersA separate cup, brush, or wheel for each grit
KitsFollow the IFU for speed, time, and coolant
MaterialsMaterial-specific lines; do not share tools across substrates
Khan et al. 2024, narrative review
How many steps?
Multi-step aluminum oxide discs most reliably reach the lowest roughness. Reduced-step systems also get under 0.2 μm. A terminal paste improves every system.
What actually drives failure
Deviating from the protocol (speed, time, coolant), more than the choice of brand.
Source: Phillips Ch. 16, Summary and Recommendations; Khan et al. 2024.

05
Movement Five
Material by Material
Same rules, different substrates. Hardness, microstructure, and heat sensitivity decide the abrasive, the speed, and the last step.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Resin Composite A Two-Phase Microstructure
Soft Matrix Plus Hard Filler Means the Surface Wears Selectively
Abrasives remove matrix faster than filler, so fillers stand proud, and filler size caps the gloss you can reach.
Step 1
Contour
12-fluted carbide, 30 to 100 μm diamond, or coarse disc. Also removes the Mylar surface: smooth, but resin-rich and stain-prone.
Step 2
Finish
16 to 30-fluted carbides, fine diamonds, white stones, medium and fine discs. Flexible discs follow convexities; thin stiff discs reach embrasures but flatten curves.
Step 3
Polish
Superfine discs, diamond-impregnated rubber, SiC brushes, then alumina or diamond paste of 5 μm or less.
Two composite-specific decisions
When: some products recommend delayed finishing while polymerization continues. Which: small-filler resin composites (nanofilled, microfilled) reach a higher gloss than large-filler hybrids.

Source: Phillips Ch. 16, Resin-Based Composite Restorations.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Resin Composite Filler Size, Shape, and Monomer Chemistry
Polishing Sets the Surface on Day One; the Filler System Decides How Long It Lasts
Ruivo, Pacheco, Sebold, Giannini 2019
Same polish, different aging
Five resin composites, same polish, then 30,000 brushing cycles and six months in water. Brushing strips matrix; irregular fillers and hydrophilic monomers roughen fastest.
Steps worth adding
A 30-fluted bur between the 12-fluted bur and the polisher improved roughness and hardness (Ehrmann et al. 2018). Diamond-only finishing left Ra above 1 μm; a full sequence cut it by 70 to 90% (Yadav et al. 2016).
Shortcuts that fail
Dry finishing changes color and opacity (Molaei et al. 2024) and the protocol changes stain resistance (Salama et al. 2025; Sarıcı and Dayı 2025). Resin sealants did not keep the surface smoother after brushing (Rios et al. 2009).
Source: Ruivo MA, Pacheco RR, Sebold M, Giannini M. Surface roughness and filler particles characterization of resin-based composites. Microsc Res Tech. 2019;82(10):1756-1767. Other studies as cited on the cards; all in vitro.

Glass-Ceramics Glass Phase and Glazing
Only Glass-Rich Ceramics Can Autoglaze, and No Glaze Hides a Rough Surface
Contacts are always polished to their smoothest state; glaze is for esthetic areas.
Option A
Natural glaze (autoglaze)
Refiring melts the ceramic's own glass into a smooth skin. Preferred: it wears less than an add-on. Only glass-rich ceramics (feldspathic, leucite); not zirconia or lithium disilicate.
Option B
Overglaze
Low-fusing glass painted on and fired. Weaker, and it wears off in function. Esthetic, nonfunctional areas only, over a surface already polished.
Option C
Mechanical polishing
Stones, then rubber polishers in two or three steps, then diamond paste on felt. Matches or beats glaze in smoothness.

Glass-Ceramics Chairside Adjustment and the Evidence
Chairside Polishing Can Equal Glazing, but Only With Ceramic-Specific Kits
Extraoral versus intraoral
Phillips, Ceramic Restorations
ExtraoralFull instrument range; heavier adjustments
IntraoralMinor roughness only; finer kits
KitsMatched to the ceramic's hardness and composition
Turkoglu et al. 2026
Four chairside protocols, four CAD-CAM glass-ceramics
Ceramic-specific kits reached Sa of about 0.33 μm on a lithium disilicate; composite kits stayed rougher. Glaze and paste polishing traded places by material.
Why studies disagree
Kit order, time, Ra versus Sa, and firing programs differ, and polishing and glazing systems change physical properties differently by material (Gökay et al. 2026; Külünk et al. 2026).
Source: Phillips Ch. 16; Turkoglu et al. 2026; Gökay et al. 2026; Külünk et al. 2026.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Polycrystalline Zirconia Sintering and Phase Transformation
Polish Zirconia in the Presintered State: Sintering Does Not Erase Milling Striations
Reason 1
Striations survive the furnace
Milling marks persist after sintering. Polish presintered and the crown leaves the furnace nearly finished.
Reason 2
Grinding transforms the surface
Grinding sintered Y-TZP triggers tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation and subsurface damage. Presintered adjustment avoids it.
Reason 3
Glaze wears through
Glaze over rough zirconia wears off and exposes a surface that severely wears opposing enamel.
The rule for contacts
Polish every contact; never rely on glaze. Polishing sintered zirconia late can also leave a pearl-like sheen.
Source: Phillips Ch. 16, Ceramic Restorations, Figs. 16-19 to 16-21; Ch. 10, Transformation Toughening.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Polycrystalline Zirconia When You Must Adjust Chairside
Intermittent Contact, Copious Water, and Zirconia-Specific Diamond Polishers
1Adjust with a fine diamond under spray, in light intermittent strokes.
2Prepolish with the coarse zirconia polisher.
3Polish with the fine and superfine polishers, lighter pressure.
4Diamond paste on brush or felt where accessible.

the hardness rule, again

A hardness story
The same grain has a smaller hardness gap to Co-Cr than to gold, so it cuts less per pass, heats more, and its binder must take more force.

Enamel, Dentin, Cementum Abrasion Resistance of Tooth Tissues
Cementum Abrades 35 Times and Dentin 25 Times Faster Than Enamel
Enamel 340 to 430 KHN; dentin about 70; cementum about 40. What is gentle on enamel is not gentle on a root.

Finishing the Preparation Bernardes, Pacheco, et al. 2026
The Prepared Tooth Is Finished Too: It Changes Roughness, Smear Layer, and Bond Strength
144 molars prepared with a medium diamond, then finished eight ways before bonding a resin-matrix glass-ceramic.
Finishing after preparationSaSmear layerμTBS
Medium diamond only (control)1.527.0 μm10.8 MPa
Fine + superfine diamond1.017.6 μm18.1 MPa
Fine + superfine carbide0.664.3 μm15.3 MPa
Ultrasonic diamond tips0.742.9 μm17.0 MPa
SiC / Al₂O₃ mounted stones0.692.5 μm28.0 MPa
Sintered diamond0.732.3 μm16.1 MPa
50 μm Al₂O₃ air abrasion1.157.3 μm19.4 MPa
Resin coating (immediate dentin sealing)1.257.3 μm32.1 MPa
Every finishing step beat the control
Mounted stones nearly tripled bond strength; resin coating did best. Clinical read: finish the prep with fine stones, or seal it immediately.
Smoother did not mean stronger
Roughness and bond strength were uncorrelated (R² = 0.004). Carbide burs gave the smoothest dentin, but microcracks and a lower bond.
Source: Bernardes P, Soares AG, de Melo BI, Pereira LM, Palma-Dibb RG, Pacheco RR, Prudente MS, Raposo LHA. Effect of finishing protocols on dentin surface characteristics and bond strength after tooth preparation for indirect restorations. J Prosthet Dent. 2026;135(2):371.e1-e11. In vitro; μTBS, microtensile bond strength.
RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Measuring Smoothness Surface Metrology
Ra Is a Line, Sa Is an Area, Gloss Is What the Patient Sees
Profilometry
Ra, Rq
A stylus traces one line; Ra is the mean deviation. It reads differently across versus along scratches.
Areal metrology
Sa
An optical map of an area; the areal Ra. Common in newer ceramic studies, one reason numbers differ.
Glossmeter
Gloss units (GU)
Reflectance at 60°: above ~70 GU is high gloss, below 10 GU matte. Ra near 0.1 μm is optically smooth.
Why one number is not enough
Below 0.2 μm, bacterial adhesion still varied with material and surface energy (Özarslan et al. 2022), and polishing method changed gingival fibroblast behavior (Ghezzi et al. 2024).
Source: ISO 4287 and ISO 25178; de Melo et al. 2022; Özarslan et al. 2022; Ghezzi et al. 2024.

RSDM 5511 Dental Materials
Summary What to Take to Clinic
Choose the Abrasive by the Substrate, and Never Skip a Step
Finishing versus polishing
Finishing shapes with medium and fine grits, one direction per grit. Polishing adds luster with grains of 5 μm or less, in every direction, with the lightest force.
Hardness and protocol
Harder grain, bigger gap, faster cut; the binder must match the substrate. Contour, finish, polish, with no skipped grits, clean carriers, and coolant.
One line per material
Resin composite: remove the Mylar layer; paste last. Amalgam: slow, fine paste at placement. Glass-ceramics: polish, glaze only nonfunctional areas. Zirconia: polish presintered. Gold: burnish, go slow. Co-Cr: stronger binders. Acrylic: pumice slurry, keep it cool. Prep and prophy: finish the prep; fine pastes on restorations.
Judge with light, not the explorer. Smooth but dull: finished, not polished. Glossy with a ledge: polished, not finished. Both go back a step.
Source: Phillips Ch. 16 and the studies cited on each slide.
